features.rationale: Phase 7, 07B: strict lambda and macro arity is now unconditional; the former opt-in divergence is closed. The condition symbol is compared on arity-not-strict and the count on arity-lambda-direct-nargs, for the closure-rendering reason recorded in phase7-arity-condition-rendering.

Tag comparison is `eq`, not `eql`/`equal` (cond-ct5-*): an equal fixnum matches, floats and strings do not, a shared cons matches while two fresh conses do not. Value delivery (cond-ct1), innermost same-tag wins (cond-ct2), and `nil` never matches as a tag (cond-ct4). The catch frame (`FeFrameCatch`) carries the gc/cleanup checkpoints the throw path drains to, and an uncaught throw raises structured `no-catch`. `(catch)` with no tag is wrong-number-of-arguments, diagnosed before anything evaluates (cond-ct-arity-catch-zero).

Phase 13.4 trap battery: catch tags are compared with `eq` and nothing about the comparison type-checks the operands, so `t` is a legal tag and a throw whose tag matches an outer catch passes through an inner one. `nil` as a tag does NOT match, on Emacs as on fe -- cond-ct4 pins that -- so the two constants are pinned separately rather than assumed symmetric. Pinned, not changed.

Phase 13.4 trap battery: `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=` are variadic and pairwise-all, not first-pair. An implementation that compares only arguments 0 and 1 answers t for (< 1 5 3); Emacs and fe answer nil. Pinned rather than changed -- fe already agreed on all six -- because the failure mode is silent wrong answers in range checks rather than an error. `=`'s chain is primitive-numeric-eq-chain-true/-false and `/=`'s strict binary arity is num-not-equal-arity, which Emacs agrees with.

Phase 6 condition handling: handlers match a static error hierarchy by symbol, list, or t; bind their optional variable to (SYMBOL . DATA); and run their bodies as an implicit sequence. Quit matches only quit or t, while budget remains uncatchable. :success is deliberately unsupported. A condition raised by a running handler bypasses that handler and searches an enclosing condition-case (cond-cc-handler-bypass).
Fe deliberately does not implement Emacs' :success handler.

Phase 6, 06A Decision 1: the hierarchy is static C data, not symbol properties, so Fe has no `get` and no `error-conditions`. On Fe's actual function channel cond-h1 is plain `void-function get`, byte-identical to a typo; there is no curated known-missing-function channel (10A Decision 5). The row is kept as the recorded oracle the static table was built against -- Emacs spells arith-error's chain as (arith-error error) -- and is `unsupported` rather than `planned` because nothing is planned: symbol properties are a later phase's question if any init-file corpus ever needs them. The hierarchy Fe does implement is exercised by cond-cc5, cond-cc8 and cond-ct6, which match a subtype through an `error` handler. Every chain Fe registered was one level deep until sub-plan 12C added `file-missing' < `file-error' < `error' (the condition-hierarchy-file-classes row below), which is the first two-deep one and the first to exercise `FindConditionParentByName''s walk past a single link; Emacs' other deeper chains (overflow-error -> range-error -> arith-error) are still excluded by the same Decision and still have no producer in Fe.

Phase 20: `end-of-buffer` and `beginning-of-buffer` join the hierarchy as children of `error` -- Emacs' own chain, measured on 31.0.90, `(get 'end-of-buffer 'error-conditions)` being `(end-of-buffer error)`. Two data lines and no code, like `file-missing` before them: the three consumers of `condition_parents` are sizeof-driven loops. What the lines buy is that `(signal 'end-of-buffer nil)` is legal at all -- `IsConditionSymbol` gates `signal` on this table and answered `Invalid error symbol` before -- and that the two carry Emacs' `error-message` text. Nothing in fe raises them; kg's motion and editing commands do, which is why they are here.

Sub-plan 12C Part 1: `file-missing' < `file-error' < `error', Emacs' own chain -- measured on 31.0.90, `(get 'file-missing 'error-conditions)' is (file-missing file-error error). `file-error' was already in the table and already worked; this adds one data line and no code, because all three consumers of `condition_parents' are sizeof-driven loops and `FindConditionParentByName' already walks the chain. It is nevertheless the FIRST two-deep entry, so it is also the first case that exercises that walk past one link -- which is why 06A Decision 1's note that `every chain Fe registers is one level deep' (the condition-hierarchy row above) no longer holds. Two things follow from the line and are pinned here: `(signal 'file-missing ...)' becomes legal, since `IsConditionSymbol' gates `signal' on this table and used to answer `(error "Invalid error symbol" file-missing)'; and a `file-missing' is caught by a `file-error' or an `error' handler while a `file-error' is NOT caught by a `file-missing' one. kg's loader and `require' raise it at their two measured sites in sub-plan 12D; nothing in fe raises it, which is deliberate -- fe's core has no file operations. `permission-denied', Emacs' third file class, is NOT implemented: it is measurable only unprivileged (this box runs the suite as root, where `chmod 000' is defeated and `(file-readable-p ...)' is t), and 12A Decision 1 records it rather than asserting it. Neither is `file-already-exists', Emacs' FOURTH -- `(get 'file-already-exists 'error-conditions)' is (file-already-exists file-error error) on 31.0.90, the same one-deep-under-file-error shape -- which a review pass noted was missing from this row and from doc/language.md. Being absent from `condition_parents' means both are refused by `signal' as well as unraisable, which is a Lisp-visible consequence and not only a missing producer: measured, `(signal 'file-already-exists '("a"))' is `(file-already-exists "a")' in Emacs and `(error "Invalid error symbol" file-already-exists)' here. Adding either is one data line, as `file-missing' was; neither is added until a producer needs it, since a catchable name nothing raises is a promise the tree cannot keep.

A condition is the cons `(SYMBOL . DATA)` constructed at signal time: `(car 5)` produces `(wrong-type-argument listp 5)`, while `(/ 1 0)` signals `(arith-error)` with no data. The rendered message remains byte-identical at existing raise sites.

Emacs protects only the value cell: `(fset 't ...)` succeeds and returns the function, and `(defalias ':k 'car)` answers `:k`. Fe extends setting-constant to function-cell writes for nil, t and keywords, which 08B's Table C chose deliberately. Nothing is lost: `t` and a keyword never resolve as a call head in Fe's evaluator, so a function stored there would be unreachable, and leaving the write to succeed would mean a symbol that is constant in one namespace and not the other.

Measured, all three rows, where 08B measured only one. Emacs binds every constant name in a lambda list and the body really sees the argument: `((lambda (t) t) 5)`, `((lambda (nil) nil) 5)` and `((lambda (:kw) :kw) 5)` are all 5. Fe follows Emacs for `t` (constant-lambda-t-shadow, supported) and refuses the other two. `nil` is not a name any Fe environment can hold -- it is a distinct object, not a symbol in the table -- so matching Emacs there would mean changing what nil is. A keyword's self-evaluation is an intern-time property of the symbol, and letting a lexical binding shadow it would make `:kw` mean different things in different scopes, which is the thing 08B set out to stop.

Emacs binds a variable literally named `&rest` and answers 2. Fe compiles a `let` binding list into a lambda application, so the name reached the parameter decoder and bound one value to a rest parameter: `(let ((&rest 1) (x 2)) x)` answered `(1 2)`. Fe now raises `lambda-list keyword in let binding` rather than meaning something else. Only `&optional` and `&rest` are refused -- any other `&`-prefixed name binds normally in both, so `(let ((&foo 1)) &foo)` is 1 either side.

Phase 8, 08B Table C: constants are protected, keywords self-evaluate and keywordp reports the intern-time property. `:` on its own is a keyword too, measured against Emacs 31.0.90 rather than guessed -- 08B's own text asked for the measurement and the implementation assumed a minimum name length of 2, leaving `:` an ordinary unbound symbol.

`error` formats its message at signal time: cond-data-error-format pins `(error "fmt %d" 7)` becoming `(error "fmt 7")`, with the rendered string as condition data. cond-q1 pins the uncaught host-boundary shape through the structured channel. The cond-err-* rows pin the format directives against Emacs: %s is princ and %S is prin1, recursively (a string keeps or loses its quotes at every level), arguments the format string never consumes are ignored, and `(error)` with no format string at all is wrong-number-of-arguments.

Phase 19: every condition symbol in the hierarchy carries Emacs' own `error-message` property, seeded when the context opens rather than kept in a C table the renderer reads directly. Two reasons, both measurable: `(get 'wrong-type-argument 'error-message)` answers on Emacs and would answer nil here, and a program can `put` its own message over one -- the renderer reads the property and nothing else. The cost is counted into `FeMinimumArenaSize` (`GetConditionMessageObjectCount`), which is exact rather than an upper bound, so the count skips a row whose symbol the primitive table already interned.

Emacs renders the `error-message` property through `substitute-quotes`, so under a curling `text-quoting-style` the three messages containing an apostrophe come out curled: measured on 31.0.90, `(error-message-string '(void-variable foo))` is `Symbol’s value as variable is void: foo` there and `Symbol's ...` here. The PROPERTY is ASCII on both sides (see `error-message-property`); only the rendering differs, and only for those three. fe has no `text-quoting-style`, no `substitute-command-keys` and no place to put one: curving is a display policy about the host's terminal, not a property of the condition. Both halves are now snapshotted against the oracle: `error-message-string-quoted-text` binds `text-quoting-style` to `grave` and fe matches Emacs exactly, and `error-message-string-curled-text` binds it to `curve` and records the divergence itself. That second snapshot was impossible until Phase 20 fixed the oracle shim, which wrote Emacs' INTERNAL representation of a raw byte to stdout and so produced a record that was not decodable UTF-8; `comparison` was kg-policy for that mechanical reason and is `emacs` now that the reason is gone. fe/test_api.c pins the ASCII text this side renders.

Phase 19 implements it, and the row that recorded its absence records its shape instead. Emacs' rendering of an ERROR object `(SYMBOL . DATA)`, written from `print_error_message` (print.c) rather than approximated: `error` and the `file-error` subtypes take their message from the DATA, everything else from the symbol's `error-message` property; items print with `prin1`, except under a `file-error` where they print with `princ`; a message that is not a string is `peculiar error` and an empty one drops the separator that would follow it. The C half is `FeErrorMessageString` (FE_API_VERSION 9 -> 10), what a host calls from inside its `FeSetErrorFn` callback; it suspends the step budget across the render, because printing is work and both the budget and the interrupt poll RAISE, which is the one thing an error callback must not do. The row's old text -- 06A: 'none is planned', a condition reaches a host as a message formatted at the raise site -- was true of a host that only ever prints; it stopped being true once kg's natives raised structured conditions (Phase 13.3) whose raise site has no sentence to format. `cond-h2`, the case that recorded the target rendering, moved to `writer-top-level-string-print`: its value is a BARE string, so what it measures now that the rendering exists is fe's top-level `print` convention rather than the rendering.

Sub-plan 12B Part 2's one deliberate divergence in `eval'. Emacs' LEXICAL argument selects an environment: `t' means lexical binding with an empty lexical environment (`(eval '(+ 1 2) t)' is 3 there) and an alist of (NAME . VALUE) pairs supplies one (`(eval 'zz '((zz . 5)))' is 5). Fe has no environment model for either -- its lexical environments are the evaluator's own chain and there is no reader or constructor for one at the Lisp level -- so a non-nil LEXICAL raises `unsupported feature: eval lexical argument' rather than being silently ignored, which is the convention `macroexpand''s ENVIRONMENT argument already set (macroexpand-environment, the sibling row). Nil and absent are the supported spellings and behave exactly as Emacs' do. Closing this means Lisp-level lexical environments, which nothing in either tree needs; it is recorded, not planned.

Phase 13.1: `signal` and `error` are ordinary functions in Emacs -- (special-form-p 'signal) is nil there -- and both arms here route to the eval-list frame, which evaluates every operand. Neither had a row in fe_eval.c's primitive_is_function[], so IsRawFormCallable() classified them as special forms and funcall/apply answered `invalid-function`. Measured before the fix, in fe and through kg's kgbatch alike: (funcall 'signal 'error (list "x")) => invalid-function signal, (apply 'error (list "boom")) => invalid-function error. The raise now carries the condition the program named and is catchable where the funcall stands. FE_LANGUAGE_VERSION 10 -> 11 for it.

Phase 13.1: `keywordp` is an ordinary predicate in Emacs and its arm here is the unary frame, which evaluates its operand, but it too had no primitive_is_function[] row -- so every higher-order use answered `invalid-function keywordp`, including (mapcar 'keywordp '(:a 1)), which kg's prelude mapcar reaches through funcall. Direct calls were never affected, which is why the gap survived a corpus that only ever calls it in call position.

Fe has no hash-table type, no reader syntax for one, and no primitives that construct or query one. Not on this program's roadmap; the compat runner short-circuits cases naming this feature instead of running them. On Fe's actual function channel `(hash-table-p ...)` is plain `void-function`, byte-identical to a typo: there is no curated known-missing-function channel (10A Decision 5).

Sub-plan 11B (11A Decision 2): the primitive that gives a symbol its special and let-dynamic flags. Emacs has no function of this name -- there the flags are set by `defvar`/`defconst`, which fe deliberately does not gain, so kg's prelude macros call this instead. kg-policy, therefore, not emacs: what is Emacs-comparable is the *behaviour* the flags produce, and the Emacs-comparison cases for that are kg's (sub-plan 11D), written against `defvar` and the same 21-probe grid.

Sub-plan 04C: `apply` spreads its final list argument into the call, so `+` is called with 1 2 3 4 and returns 10. Implemented as an evaluate-then-redispatch on the frame stack (the plan's chosen shape, see doc/implementation.md); a non-list final operand is `apply: last argument must be a proper list`.

Sub-plan 04C designator rule, timing: function-cell symbol indirection is resolved at call time, not at defalias time -- `a` is aliased to `b` before `b` gets a function, and calling `(a)` afterwards still returns 1. FeGetFunction (the host API, 04C) follows that same chain.

Sub-plan 04C: `defalias` points one symbol's function cell at another symbol, and call-position resolution follows the designator chain, so `(first (list 1 2))` behaves like `car` and returns 1; `defalias` returns the aliased symbol (first), per the 04A snapshot.

Phase 4 primitive `fboundp` (04C) asks the function namespace; the 04D cut moved the bootstrap into function cells, so the primitive `car`'s function cell is occupied and `(fboundp 'car)` is t, matching the 04A-pinned oracle. The pre-cut answer was nil because `car` still lived in a value cell.
Sub-plan 04C: `fmakunbound` empties only the function cell, so the subsequent call is void-function j. The pair with the two keeps-* cases pins that the unbound operations act on disjoint cells.

Sub-plan 04C cell separation, mirror arm: `fmakunbound` leaves the value cell alone, so the bare symbol still evaluates to 1. Together with lisp2-makunbound-keeps-function it records that unbounding one namespace never touches the other.

Sub-plan 04C: `fset` evaluates both arguments -- the first is a value naming the target symbol, not a quote -- so the symbol named by `s` (k) receives the function and `(k)` returns 4. Sub-plan 04E has since landed: kg's prelude defines its 52 functions in the function namespace, respelled from the old `setq` forms to `defalias`, `fset`'s sibling primitive writing the same cell.

What `funcall`/`apply` may be handed: a function, never a macro or a special form, which Emacs signals invalid-function for. Fe's evaluate-then-redispatch shape makes this a correctness requirement rather than a nicety -- the redispatched `(callable (quote v) ...)` form reaches a raw-form callable as the wrappers themselves, so `(funcall 'quote 'a)` answered `(quote a)` and `(funcall 'if 1 2 3)` chose a branch of quoted forms. The classification is read off the evaluator's own primitive routing and is exposed to hosts as the C API's FeIsFunction().

Sub-plan 04C: a symbol passed to `funcall` is a designator resolved through its function cell, following the same indirection call-position lookup uses, so `(funcall 'g)` calls the fset'd lambda and returns 9. A self-referential chain dies with cyclic-function-indirection rather than exhausting the step budget.

Phase 4 primitive `funcall` (04C): it takes a *value*, here a lexical closure, so the function cell of the name is irrelevant. The funcall machinery itself is complete; what the comparison still waits on is the case's Emacs-shaped `let` bindings list, which fe's bare-symbol `let` cannot read -- not 04E, which has landed. An Emacs-shaped `let` in fe's core is Phase 8 Wave A of the kg plan set (the same blocker as lisp2-let-no-function-shadow).

Which name a dead designator chain is reported at: the one the program wrote, not the last link the resolver reached. Emacs answers `void-function chain-head` for both `(chain-head)` and `(funcall 'chain-head)`; fe's call position always did, and its funcall arm named the tail until the resolver stopped reporting a `dead` link at all.

Sub-plan 04C: `(function (lambda ...))` is a raw-form special form producing a real closure value -- not a designator -- and `funcall` calls it directly, returning 3. Since the 04D reader change, `#'(lambda ...)` reads as this same form (reader-sharp-quote-identity). Known gap, deliberate and unsnapshotted: fe accepts only a symbol or a lambda/fn form, so `(function 5)` is `unsupported-function-form`, where Emacs' `function` is plain `quote` and answers 5. Fe rejects what it cannot make a callable out of rather than quietly handing back a non-function, and the 04A pin names that spelling; a case for it would record a divergence nobody intends to close.

Phase 4 designator rule for `functionp`: a symbol whose function cell holds a function is t, an unbound name is nil, never an error. The blocker is not 04E (landed) but that fe has no `functionp` primitive at all, so the comparison still fails on void-function functionp. Fe now exposes the predicate to its hosts as the C API's FeIsFunction() -- the designator chain, macros and special forms answered exactly as Emacs' `functionp` answers them -- and the row flips when a Lisp-callable `functionp` exists, whether fe grows the primitive or kg's native is rewritten onto FeIsFunction().

Phase 4 semantics, value namespace only: `let` binds names in the value namespace and must not shadow a function of the same spelling, so `(car (list 1 2))` still resolves the primitive. Fe's `let` primitive takes a bare symbol, so the Emacs-shaped bindings list is a separate, already-divergent shape (primitive-let); the function-cell side of the split is what this case pins. Not flippable yet, and 04E (now landed) was never the blocker: fe cannot read the Emacs-shaped bindings list this case is written in at all, because fe's own `let` takes a bare symbol. That lands when an Emacs-shaped `let` moves into fe's core -- Phase 8 Wave A of the kg plan set -- and this row flips with it.

kg-policy representation divergence, recorded by Phase 4's own plan (04A): Emacs stores a macro as a (macro . FUNCTION) cons in the function cell, observable only through (symbol-function 'NAME); fe has a distinct FeTMacro type and prints a macro value as (macro PARAMS BODY). Pinned by fe/test_api.c's TestWriter, which already asserts '(macro (a) a)' renders '(macro (a) a)'. The Phase 4 function-cell work (04C) must not imitate the cons representation to pass a case nobody wrote yet; this is kg-policy because Emacs has no anonymous macro object to snapshot at all.
Sub-plan 04C cell separation: `makunbound` acts on the value cell only, leaving the function cell intact, so `(m)` still returns 2. One half of the disjointness the split must preserve.

Sub-plan 04C: `symbol-function` returns the function cell's object -- a designator stays a symbol -- and `funcall` calls it, so the roundtrip returns 5. The printed-closure question is avoided by comparing behaviour, per 04A's data decision.

Phase 4 primitive `symbol-value` (04C) reads the value cell directly; the explicit read of a setq'd name agrees, and the mirror arm `lisp2-symbol-value-primitive` passed once the 04D cut emptied the primitive `car`'s value cell, so `(symbol-value 'car)` signals void-variable -- the explicit-value-namespace mirror of one-namespace-boundp's nil.

Sub-plan 04C, the phase's headline: a symbol holds a value (7) and a function (an fset'd lambda) at once, call position resolves the function cell, bare-symbol evaluation the value cell, and (list f (f)) is (7 9). 04D then moved the bootstrap into function cells and deleted the value-cell fallback; this case's comparison is unchanged by the cut.

Sub-plan 04C call-position semantics, sharpened by the 04D cut: call position resolves the function cell and an empty cell is void-function -- naming the head symbol -- even when the value cell is full. Reported as FeHandleError()'s message text (the parent plan's message-level rule until Phase 6), which is how the runner matches the oracle's structured void-function condition.

Sub-plan 10B: one expansion step, returned and never evaluated. The alias cases are the ones that had to be measured rather than derived. Emacs rewrites the head one `defalias` link at a time, so `macroexpand-1` through a two-link chain answers the middle link -- not what resolving the chain the way call position does would give -- and it rewrites at all only when the target is itself a macro, so an alias to a function or to an unbound name leaves the form untouched. fe's own policy fills the one gap Emacs has no answer for: an alias ring, which Emacs' `defalias` refuses to build, raises `cyclic-function-indirection` here exactly as a call to it does (pinned in test_api.c:TestMacroexpandBudget and scripts/macroexpand.fe, not by an oracle case).

Sub-plan 10B / 10A Decision 2, deliberate and recorded in TODO.md: expanding every sub-form needs a code walker that knows the shape of each special form, which fe does not have. The name exists as a primitive purely so that calling it raises `unsupported feature: macroexpand-all` -- naming the missing feature, the reader's own reject-by-name convention -- rather than `void-function`, which is byte-identical to what a typo produces (10A Decision 5). The runner short-circuits this entry and never invokes fe; test_api.c:TestMacroexpandPrimitives and scripts/macroexpand.fe pin the raise itself.

Sub-plan 10B, deliberate: fe accepts the ENVIRONMENT operand and requires it to be nil. Emacs' environments are an internal alist that shadows the function cell for the duration of one expansion -- a second name-resolution path, which nothing in this program uses. A non-nil value is rejected by name (`unsupported feature: macroexpand environment`) instead of being silently ignored, so the divergence is loud rather than an answer computed as if the argument were not there.

Sub-plan 10B: Emacs' fixpoint rule -- keep taking single steps while the result is still a macro call. Bounded by the host's evaluation-step budget like all evaluation, so a self-expanding macro ends at `evaluation step limit exceeded`; that half has no oracle case because Emacs hangs on it and is pinned in test_api.c:TestMacroexpandBudget. A `defalias` ring is different: Fe detects it during function-cell resolution and raises `cyclic-function-indirection` immediately (Emacs refuses to create the ring, so this is Fe policy rather than an oracle result).

Sub-plan 10B: a transformer applied through `macroexpand-1`/`macroexpand` goes through the evaluator's own `EnterMacroBody`, so strict arity is the same check with the same count as a direct macro call. The FUNCTION element of the condition data renders differently on the two sides, which phase7-arity-condition-rendering already records; this case compares the symbol and the count only.
Phase 5, row A7, landed at 05D's cut: mixed addition promotes to float and prints `3.0` -- the 05D printer's `.0` guarantee, on top of 05C's promotion rule.

Phase 5, rows C1/C4/C5, landed after 05D: a chained comparison stops at the first false pair, Emacs' `arithcompare_driver` rule, so `(< 2 1 "a")` and `(= 1 2 "a")` are nil and the string is never type-checked -- while `(< 1 2 "a")` and `(= 1 1 "a")`, true up to the bad operand, do reach it and are `wrong-type-argument` on both sides. Both shapes are pinned deliberately: an implementation that simply stopped type-checking the tail would satisfy the first pair of cases and fail the second. Only the check short-circuits; every operand *form* was evaluated before the comparison arm ran.

Phase 5, row C1/C5's arity edge, landed after 05D: a single operand is `t` for `=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` and `>=`, with no type check at all, because a chain of one has no adjacent pair to compare. fe validated that one operand up front and answered `wrong-type-argument` where Emacs answers `t`; the check is gone and the comparator loop now expresses the rule by construction. `/=` is the exception and has its own case on the num-not-equal row -- it is binary, so one operand is `wrong-number-of-arguments`.
Phase 5, row C5 (05C, landed): comparison type errors say wrong-type-argument, replacing the expected-double texts on the numeric family. 05A Decision 5.
Phase 5, row A4 (05C, landed): a mixed integer/float division promotes to float -- 3.5, not 3. The tower's single promotion rule.
Phase 5, row A3, landed at 05D's cut: integer division truncates toward zero -- `(/ 7 2)` is 3 and `(/ -7 2)` is -3, reachable at last because the literals read as integers.
Phase 5, row A5, landed at 05D's cut: integer division by zero is `arith-error`, reachable at last because `1` and `0` read as integers (carried in FeHandleError()'s message until Phase 6).

Phase 5, rows E1-E3, landed at 05D's cut: fe-core `eq` is pointer identity or both-integers-equal -- `(eq 3 3)` t, `(eq 3.0 3.0)` nil (boxed floats), `(eq "a" "a")` nil. 05E deletes kg's prelude alias of `is` in the pin commit.
Phase 5, row C4 (05C, landed): numeric `=` is mathematical value equality across types -- 3 equals 3.0. The extended chained `=` arm.
Phase 5, rows E4-E5, landed at 05D's cut: fe-core `eql` is `eq` or same-type numbers equal by bits -- `(eql 3 3.0)` nil (type-strict), `(eql 0.0 -0.0)` nil (the sign bit differs).

Phase 5, row E6: the kg prelude `equal` rewrite target -- strings -> string=, numbers -> eql, else eq. Lands in 05E; standalone fe has no `equal`, so this stays a planned target snapshot in fe's corpus.
Phase 5, row M2, landed at 05D's cut: expt's per-signature rule from 05C, with the float column printing `256.0` at last via the 05D printer.
Phase 5, row P2, landed at 05D's cut: floats print shortest-round-trip, not %.7g noise -- `0.1` prints `0.1` (Decision 4's dtoastr-style loop).
Phase 5, row C2 (05C, landed): the new comparators `>` and `>=` chain too -- (t t). Both are fe core primitives sharing the comparator loop with `<`/`<=`/`=`.
Phase 5, row R9, landed at 05D's cut: `9007199254740993` reads and prints exactly -- int64 exactness past 2^53 (Decision 3's integer reader on top of 05B's object).

Phase 5, row A8's reader sibling (05A Decision 3): an integer literal that overflows int64 reads as a double -- the pre-bignum Emacs behaviour -- while modern Emacs reads it as a bignum. 2^64 (= 18446744073709551616) is the canonical example: Emacs prints the bignum 18446744073709551616, fe reads the nearest double and prints its shortest round-trip. The alternative -- a read error -- would punish pasted constants. The fall-back is bounded by the reader's token buffer, not by magnitude: `ReadAtom`'s `char buf[64]` caps a token at 63 characters, so a literal of 64 or more digits is `symbol too long` and never reaches the classifier at all. 2^64 is 20 digits and is well inside that; a caller who pastes a 64-digit constant gets a reader error rather than a double, and this row does not claim otherwise.
Phase 5, row C1 (05C, landed): `<` is variadic and chained -- (t nil). The comparator loop compares every adjacent pair; the pre-tower binary arm ignored the third operand and answered (t t).
Phase 5, row A6 (05C, landed): all-integer arithmetic stays integer -- (* 2 3) is the integer 6. The tower's integer-preserving combine.

Sub-plan 12C Part 2, closing the approximation Phase 11 recorded and said could not be closed. A let-dynamic-only mark -- what Emacs' ONE-argument `(defvar v)' sets, and what `internal--mark-special' with a nil FULL-P sets here -- is now scoped to the input unit that made it. `EvaluateInput' takes the next number of a monotone counter on the way in and hands the enclosing one back on the way out, so nested units stack; the registry entry grew a third slot holding that number, and `SymbolIsLetDynamic' compares it for EQUALITY with the ambient one. A full mark (Emacs' two-argument `defvar', and `defconst') carries no scope and stays global, which is Emacs' rule too, and `special-variable-p' answers exactly what it answered before. MEASURED on Emacs 31.0.90 with real files, lexical-binding: t, 2026-08-07: file A's one-argument defvar makes `let' over the name dynamic in A and LEXICAL in a file B loaded afterwards; a file C that A loads does not see A's mark; A does not see C's after C returns; A's own mark survives the nested load; and each `eval' is its own scope. Equality is what gives all five -- a `>=' test would let an outer unit's mark reach a nested load, which the B-loads-D probe measured false. TWO RESIDUALS, recorded rather than defended. FIRST, and the important one: Emacs' mechanism is not a per-unit registry at all. A one-argument `(defvar v)' adds v to the LEXICAL ENVIRONMENT being threaded through the file, and a `lambda' captures it -- measured, a `defun' written BEFORE the defvar in the same file binds v lexically, one written after it binds v dynamically even when it is called from another file. Fe consults the flag where the `let' RUNS and has nowhere to record a closure's unit, so it answers those two by execution site rather than by definition site. Against the five-probe grid this model is right where the old global one was wrong (the other file, and both directions of a nested load) and wrong where the old one was right (a function defined after the defvar in unit A and called from unit B: Emacs and the old model say dynamic, this says lexical). That case is NARROWER than Emacs, which is the direction the Phase 11 row warned about, and it is the reason the host-context rule below exists. Closing it means the marking becoming a lexical-environment entry -- a different and larger design, in fe_eval.c rather than fe.c. SECOND: one registry entry per symbol, so re-marking a symbol already marked let-dynamic-only RE-STAMPS its scope instead of adding an entry. Last mark wins. That keeps the registry bounded by the number of marked symbols, as it has always been, rather than growing by a cell pair every time a file that declares a name is loaded again; the edge it loses is an outer unit's mark surviving a nested unit that declares the same name. THE HOST-CONTEXT RULE: outside any input unit -- `ctx->input_scope' 0, which is a `FeCall' into a callable, a host-driven `let', or the predicate asked straight from C -- every mark is visible. There is no unit there for a mark to be foreign to, and answering no would narrow the host's view of names a file legitimately declared, including kg's hook and process callbacks. It also means fe's own standalone driver, which never enters an input unit, sees no scoping at all -- which is what scope-carrier-host-context pins, and why the scoping itself is tested in test_api.c and not in this corpus. THE UNWIND GUARANTEE, corrected by the Phase 12 fix cycle after an acceptance review measured it. The paragraph above and the comment in fe_run.c both used to present the two containment barriers as the whole answer for an abnormal exit ("this is the abnormal path, and it is the one that matters"), and that was false: they cover the CONTAINED abnormal exit only. An UNCONTAINED raise -- one that reaches `TransferEvaluationError' and the host `error_fn', i.e. every use of `FeEvaluateStringWithOptions'/`FeEvaluateFileWithOptions', which is how kg reaches `M-:', `eval-buffer', `eval-last-sexp' and `init.el' -- `longjmp's past `EvaluateInput''s restore AND past both barriers, and left the abandoned unit's number in `ctx->input_scope' for the life of the context. All three abnormal kinds leaked it (error, quit, budget), and the consequence went both ways: a mark a legitimately loaded file made became INVISIBLE in host context, where the rule below promises every mark is visible, and the abandoned unit's marks became permanently visible there. One mistyped `M-:' inverted the answers for the rest of a kg session. WHAT IS GUARANTEED NOW, on all three paths and all three abnormal kinds: a NORMAL return restores the enclosing unit (`EvaluateInput'); a CONTAINED abnormal exit restores the enclosing unit (`FeTryCallWithOptions', `FeTryEvaluateStringWithOptions'); an UNCONTAINED abnormal exit LEAVES FOR THE HOST CONTEXT -- scope 0, no source label -- rather than restoring anything, because every unit between the raise and the host is being abandoned at once and there is nothing left to go back to. The fix is `EnterHostInputContext' in `RaiseCompletionCore''s host-exit block, beside the `ClearEvaluationControl' that is there for exactly the same reason: the wrappers' own epilogues do not run on that path. The scope number and the diagnostic label are one value (`FeInputUnit') and are saved and restored together, which closed a second, pre-existing leak in the same shape: the containment barriers put the scope back but not the label, so every later diagnostic in an enclosing file that had contained a failed nested load came out with no file name at all. `test_api.c:TestOneArgDefvarScope' now covers both halves -- the contained case is named as contained, and the uncontained case probes the host-context rule with an `FeCall' from C before and after each of the three abnormal kinds, and asserts `input_scope' is 0. A Fe string is a byte string, built by appending at strlen, so a string escape has to land in one byte. Emacs holds a NUL like any other character and reads `"\400"` as U+0100 and `"\x41f"` as U+041F. Before 08C's repair Fe wrote (char)value into that buffer: a decoded NUL was a silent no-op that shifted the rest of the string down -- `(list "\0a" "a\0b")` answered `("a" "ab")` -- and anything above 255 was truncated into the same hole. All three are named read errors now, which is the rule the reader already applied to a literal NUL byte in the source text. Matching Emacs instead would need a length-carrying string representation and a multibyte character type, neither of which is funded here. The character-literal forms of the same escapes agree with Emacs exactly (reader-char-hex-greedy, reader-char-octal-nul); it is only a string body that is byte-limited.

Emacs allows character modifiers inside a string body, folding `"\C-a"` to the control character and storing `"\M-a"` as the raw byte 0341 in a unibyte string. Fe implements the modifier chain for `?` literals only: in a string body `\C` reaches the escape table, finds nothing and errors. Half-implementing it would be worse than not -- the 2^27 meta bit has no byte representation, so accepting `"\M-a"` would mean inventing Emacs' unibyte high-bit convention on top of a byte string that already cannot hold a character above 255 (reader-string-byte-limit).

Both sides read `"\377"` to the same thing -- the byte 0377 -- and disagree only in the printed record: Emacs' prin1 re-escapes it as \377 for a unibyte string, Fe's writer emits the raw byte. A printer divergence, the same class as writer-bounded-output, recorded here because the octal escape family is otherwise compared as supported.

Emacs is permissive about escapes it does not know: `"\q"` is "q" (the backslash is dropped), `"\ "` and a backslash-newline continuation both produce nothing, and `"\N{U+41}"` is "A". Fe rejects each by name. 08C's plan text made this choice explicitly -- an init-file dialect earns strictness -- and the reason is that silently dropping a backslash is how a typo in a regexp or a path becomes a wrong string instead of a diagnostic. `\N{...}` additionally needs a Unicode name table Fe does not carry; its `U+` form is a second spelling of `\x`.

Phase 14 implements Emacs' symbol escapes, superseding the named rejection this row recorded from 08C to Phase 13. A backslash takes the next byte into the name literally -- `a\ b` is the one symbol "a b" and `\1` is the symbol "1" -- and one escape anywhere in a token suppresses the number classification for the whole token. The rejection it replaces was itself a repair: a backslash was refused only at a token's first character, so `(a\ b)` read as the two symbols `a` and `b` and cdr answered `(b)`, a silent misread of the list's length. What is still rejected is a backslash with nothing after it -- `unterminated symbol escape` -- and the strict-reader policy for everything Phase 14 did not deliberately open (vectors, `#` syntax other than `##`, unknown string escapes) is unchanged.

Phase 14: an escaped dot is an ordinary list element where a bare one is the dotted-tail marker, so `(a \. b)` is a three-element list and `(a . b)` is a pair. Both spellings read to the same interned symbol, so the object alone cannot tell them apart -- the reader records whether the token it just produced contained an escape, and the dotted-tail test consults that. Without it the escape would have turned a three-element list into a pair, silently.

A fe string is a BYTE string -- the reader-string-byte-limit family's rule -- so `length', `aref' and `elt' answer bytes where Emacs' character strings answer characters. ASCII agrees; anything above it does not. Phase 24 is the first time a fe program could ask the question; the representation that would change the answer is Phase 25's. source_name is null: `length' is claimed by primitive-length.

`signal` builds `(SYMBOL . DATA)` at raise time and the data reaches the handler verbatim (cond-s1); a non-symbol condition is `wrong-type-argument` with `symbolp` data (cond-s2); an unregistered condition symbol becomes `(error "Invalid error symbol" SYMBOL)` catchable by an `(error ...)` handler (cond-s3); improper data is tolerated (cond-s4).

Fe's `signal` accepts registered static-hierarchy names, including `quit`; `(signal 'quit nil)` has a structured quit completion. The compatibility runner compares that completion without relying on diagnostic text.
Phase 20: `string>` is `string<` with the operands the other way round, which is how Emacs defines `string-greaterp` too. One extra arm in the binary resume and no second implementation of the order.

Phase 20: Emacs' `string<`, taking a string or a SYMBOL on either side and comparing by character. fe compares by BYTE and the two agree for every string either dialect can hold, because UTF-8 preserves codepoint order under byte-lexicographic comparison -- `string-order-codepoints` is that claim asked at the boundary that would show it. The implementation is `StringOperandLess` in fe.c, a cell at a time over the chunked string representation, which `string-order-cells` exercises at both kinds of cell boundary; the NUL padding of a short last cell is what makes a prefix sort first with no length test, since `memcmp` already orders NUL before every real byte. It arrives as a primitive rather than as kg prelude Lisp because kg's `apropos` sorts with it and a per-character prelude comparison spent an evaluation's whole step budget on 35 names.

Phase 14: all eight names are ordinary functions -- `(special-form-p 'intern)` is nil on Emacs -- and evaluate every operand, so they are reachable through `funcall` and `apply`. Phase 13 had to repair exactly this for `signal`, `error` and `keywordp`, whose missing `primitive_is_function[]` rows made them look like special forms; the family lands with its rows from the start.

Phase 14: `gensym` is `make-symbol` over a per-context sequence number -- the mechanism a macro's temporary needs so a user's `defvar` of the same name cannot capture it. What is pinned is uniqueness and uninternedness, not the NAME: Emacs' counter is the Lisp variable `gensym-counter` and fe's is a context field with no Lisp spelling, so a case comparing the name would be comparing two unrelated pieces of process state. Two further divergences are recorded rather than pinned, both trivial and both untested for the same reason: fe has no `gensym-counter` to read or set, and fe's PREFIX must be a string where Emacs formats any object (`(gensym 5)` is the symbol `54` there, its answer depending on the counter).

Phase 14: `get` reads a property back, answering nil for one nobody set and for a symbol with no property list at all. `(get nil 'x)` is nil too, which is why `get` tests for fe's nil before type-checking.

Phase 14: `intern` is the obarray's constructor -- by name, so two interns of one name are one object. `(intern "nil")` answers the nil object rather than minting a second thing that prints `nil`, which is the same answer Emacs gives for a different reason (its nil IS a symbol). A name longer than 63 bytes is a named error, the reader's own token bound.

Emacs' `intern` and `intern-soft` take an optional OBARRAY; fe has exactly one obarray and no way to name a second, so a second operand is `wrong-number-of-arguments`. Refusing it is the deliberate half: accepting and ignoring an OBARRAY would make a program that meant a private obarray silently share the global one, which is the class of silent misreading the strict reader exists to avoid. `make-symbol` is what a program that wanted a private name can use instead.

Phase 14, the contract this family is easiest to get wrong on: `intern-soft` answers nil on a miss and interns nothing. The double probe is what pins it -- an implementation that interns on a miss answers the symbol the second time, and the `(while (setq x (intern-soft (format ...))) ...)` idiom then allocates without bound instead of terminating. It takes a symbol as well as a string, and for a symbol the question is identity: an uninterned symbol answers nil even when a symbol of that name is interned.

Phase 14: `make-symbol` builds a symbol in no obarray. Two decisions are recorded here because they are policy rather than consequence. PRINTING: an uninterned symbol writes its bare name, which is what Emacs does with `print-gensym` nil, its default; fe has no `print-gensym` and no `#:` spelling at all, so printing is not injective for uninterned symbols on either side and the two agree on the output. COMPARISON: identity only -- `eq` is pointer identity, and fe has no `equal` of its own, kg's prelude `equal` bottoming out in `eq` for atoms, so an uninterned symbol is equal to nothing but itself. An uninterned symbol named like a keyword is an ordinary symbol, which needed `keywordp` to ask whether the interner self-bound the name rather than only whether it starts with a colon.

Phase 14: `symbol-name` reads a symbol's name back as a string, and a non-symbol raises `(wrong-type-argument symbolp X)`. fe's nil is its own object type rather than a symbol, so the name "nil" is answered for it explicitly; that is what Emacs' symbol nil answers.

Phase 14: `symbol-plist` is the whole list, which is what makes `put`'s order and overwriting observable at all. It also carries this family's storage decision: the property list lives in the SYMBOL OBJECT -- Phase 14 widened a symbol's name slot into `(name . plist)`, costing one cons per symbol -- rather than in a context-side registry in the shape the special-variable list uses. A registry keyed by symbol would keep alive every symbol that ever carried a property, and an uninterned symbol is the first symbol fe has that the collector may reclaim.

Phase 14: `put` writes a property on a symbol. Two measured behaviours rather than assumed ones: a new property is appended at the TAIL of the list (the head is the cheaper implementation and gives the other order), and an existing property is overwritten in place rather than shadowed by a second copy. Properties compare by `eq`, so an integer property works.

Emacs' nil is an ordinary symbol and carries a property list like any other, so `(put nil 'a 1)` stores and `(get nil 'a)` reads it back. fe's nil is a distinct object type with no storage of its own, so `put` refuses it by name -- `(wrong-type-argument symbolp nil)` -- rather than accepting the write and dropping it, and `get` keeps answering nil. The reading half therefore agrees with Emacs for every program that did not write; only a program that writes on nil sees the difference, and it sees a diagnostic rather than a value that quietly went missing.

An uncaught throw signals structured `(no-catch TAG VALUE)` through the ordinary error path (cond-ct3), which an enclosing `condition-case` can handle. A throw that matches a catch drains to the catch frame's checkpoint (`RunCleanupsDownTo`); the native re-entry boundary is a tested wall. `throw` is function-shaped, exactly two arguments evaluated normally, matching Emacs' `(special-form-p 'throw)` nil. One operand or three is wrong-number-of-arguments (cond-ct-arity-throw-one, cond-ct-arity-throw-three): a missing value is not nil and a third operand is not dropped.

This is the parent plan's own example of a divergence-from-Fe that is an agreement-with-Emacs: kg's fe fork changed vanilla Fe's historical behavior (silently returning nil for an unbound symbol) specifically to match Emacs's void-variable signal, and doc/fe-upstream.md's divergence table records that as a deliberate, already-landed change, not a Phase 2+ item. Status is `supported` because the oracle comparison is what this manifest tracks; the vanilla-Fe distinction is prose context only, not a comparison axis this schema has a field for.

Sub-plan 12B Part 1, closing the gap Phase 11 carried forward -- and which the Phase 12 audit measured to be broader than Phase 11 recorded. The symptom was `a cleanup that handles its own error clobbers the in-flight condition'; the defect was that a `condition-case' established inside an `unwind-protect' CLEANUP handled nothing at all, drain or no drain, so every error in a cleanup body behaved as if unhandled. `(unwind-protect 'body (condition-case nil (car 6) (error nil)))' is `body' in Emacs 31.0.90 and escaped to the host here. One ordering caused it: `RaiseCompletionCore' tested `cleanup_catch' and bounced to `RunOneCleanupEntry' before it ever called `FindConditionHandler'. The fix runs the search first and accepts a handler only at or above `cleanup_frame_floor', the frame index the running cleanup entry started at. `run_base' could not serve as that floor: a Lisp cleanup's forms republish it, a NATIVE cleanup's do not, and neither does the window before `RunEvaluationBody''s loop starts, so without the floor a native cleanup's raise could transfer to a handler outside the `unwind-protect' with the drain in the wrong state. For a native cleanup the floor equals the frame index the entry started at, and what is above it depends on what the cleanup does -- a distinction 12B Part 1 did not make and Phase 12's fix cycle corrected. A native cleanup that honours `FeCleanupFn''s contract (`fe.h': "must not call back into the evaluator") pushes no frames at all, so no handler is ever accepted and that arm IS bit-identical; `TestNativeCleanupHandlerFloor''s first three cases are that assertion and pass unchanged on the commit before the fix. A native cleanup that VIOLATES the contract by re-entering the evaluator does push frames above the floor, and a `condition-case' established in that Lisp is now honored where before it was not: measured, `(condition-case o (with-lisp-cleanup (fn () 'body) (fn () (condition-case e (car 6) (error 'inner)))) (error (list 'outer o)))' answered `(outer (wrong-type-argument listp 6))' before 95965f0 and answers `body' now. That is the desirable answer and not a native special case: it is this floor's own rule -- a handler established by the cleanup's OWN work belongs to the cleanup, not to the computation the drain is abandoning -- and it is what the pure-Lisp `unwind-protect' analogue and Emacs 31.0.90 both answer. It is unreachable from kg, whose four `FeProtectWithCleanup' handlers are pure C state restores that evaluate nothing, and it is out of contract; it is pinned anyway, by the last three cases of `TestNativeCleanupHandlerFloor', because the bit-identity claim was being offered as the argument for the fix's safety. `catch'/`throw' inside a cleanup already worked and is unaffected.

Phase 6, 06A Decision 4, complete: a cleanup runs on the error, throw and quit paths alike (cond-u1-*), nested cleanups run innermost-first (cond-u3-order), and a cleanup that raises replaces the completion already unwinding -- an error (cond-u2) or a throw (cond-u4-*), including a throw whose catch lies below the cleanup's own nested run, which is re-issued in the enclosing context rather than answered as no-catch. The five original rows were written in Emacs' progn/push and died on void-function before testing anything; their replacements are in the dialect intersection and carry fresh snapshots of their own. Re-measured against Emacs 31.0.90 by sub-plan 12B Part 1 and pinned as permanent guards, because the handler-visibility fix in that slice had to leave this policy untouched and now has three cases saying so: cond-u6-unhandled-during-error, cond-u6-unhandled-during-quit and cond-u6-cleanup-throw-during-error are the audit's probes A10, A15 and A16, and their answers are byte-identical before and after the fix. The line the fix draws is `unhandled`: a raise a cleanup's OWN handler catches never leaves the cleanup and so replaces nothing (unwind-protect-cleanup-handlers), while a raise no handler at or above the cleanup's frame floor can take still replaces the completion being unwound, exactly as this row has always said.

Two divergences in 06A Decision 4's replacement rule -- the rule the `unwind-protect-cleanup-handlers' row above says is `measured correct against Emacs on every probe' and which doc/implementation.md and doc/language.md stated unconditionally. Both are PRE-EXISTING: byte-identical on every revision since the replacement rule was implemented, unchanged by sub-plan 12B Part 1, and DISCOVERED POST-CLOSE, by the acceptance review that re-measured this area rather than by the phase that wrote about it. The rule itself holds -- an unhandled cleanup raise does replace the completion being unwound, and the remaining cleanups do still run -- and what diverges is WHERE the replacement is delivered. (1) Emacs delivers it to the ENCLOSING handler; fe delivers it to a `condition-case' established in the ABANDONED BODY if that frame is still on the stack. Measured on 31.0.90, lexical-binding: t, 2026-08-07: `(condition-case o (catch 'tg (unwind-protect (condition-case nil (throw 'tg 'body) (error 'IN)) (error "cleanup"))) (error (list 'OUT o)))' is `(OUT (error "cleanup"))' there and `IN' here. (2) The throw twin: a cleanup's `throw' can reach a `catch' the in-flight completion had already exited. `(catch 'a (unwind-protect (catch 'b (throw 'a 1)) (throw 'b 2)))' is `(no-catch b 2)' there and 2 here. ONE CAUSE, on both: `RunOneCleanupEntry' replays the cleanup's completion after restoring the frame stack the drain STARTED FROM, which still holds the abandoned computation's handler and catch frames, while Emacs unwinds as it goes and no longer has them to match. Closing it means discarding frames as the drain descends rather than at the replay, which is a different unwind model and not a bug fix; it is recorded here, qualified in doc/language.md and doc/implementation.md, and pinned by `scripts/unwind-cleanup-handler.fe' so a change of answer is visible. Note that fe's answer to (2) is the direct consequence of a rule doc/language.md states positively and deliberately -- `a catch the original throw was on its way past is still a candidate for the cleanup's own throw' -- so this row is what makes that rule's disagreement with Emacs explicit rather than implicit.

Phase 24: `[...]' is vector read syntax and the writer emits the same syntax back, so a vector round-trips through print and read. This row is the flip of the vector third of reader-hash-syntax-unsupported, which recorded the rejection it replaces.

Both sides reject `[1 . 2]' and only the condition symbol differs: Emacs raises `invalid-read-syntax' and fe raises its own named read error, the same shape of disagreement reader-character-delimiter already records. Phase 8's rule for this reader is reject rather than misread, and accepting the dot would silently produce the three-element vector [1 \. 2].

Phase 24: input that stops inside a vector raises `end-of-file' with nil data, which is Emacs' generic incomplete-input condition and was measured before fe had one. The same condition now names an unclosed LIST, whose message text is unchanged.
Fe reports `void-function` as a structured, catchable condition; every recorded Fe-side result therefore carries condition_source: "structured".

This is kg/fe's own deliberate policy, not an Emacs contract: the parent kg repository's CLAUDE.md already states the precedent for exactly this shape of decision (kg_regex_match_backward's backward-matching policy is kg's own, not Emacs', so an oracle for it would have to encode kg's policy rather than read Emacs'), and 00b-oracle-and-differential-corpus.md's own 'What this does not do' names cyclic-structure printing explicitly. Pinned by fe/test_api.c's TestWriter, which already asserts all three bounded forms (#<cycle>, #<deep>, #<truncated>). PHASE 24: a vector inherits this policy unchanged rather than acquiring one of its own. A vector that contains itself terminates in the writer's existing depth bound and prints nested brackets ending in `#<deep>', exactly as a list whose car is itself already did; Emacs prints the lossy back-reference `[0 #0]' at its `print-circle' default and the re-readable `#1=[0 #1#]' with `print-circle' bound to t. Adopting `#N' would need an ancestor stack in every `Writer' -- including the one `RenderErrorMessage' runs on the error path -- and would buy a spelling that still does not read back. doc/language.md states the decision; fe/test_api.c's TestVectors asserts the bounded shape.

Phase 19: `prin1` escapes both bytes the reader would otherwise take for itself, the closing quote and the backslash. Until this the writer escaped only the quote, so `(list "x\\y")` printed `(x\y)` and read back as `xy` -- the one printed form fe had left that was not re-readable, and visible from kg since `regexp-quote`. Recorded in kg's doc/TODO.md from Phase 14 with `whichever phase next touches the writer` as its stated home; this is that phase, because `error-message-string` prints its data items with `prin1`.

Phase 14: a symbol whose name would otherwise read back as something else prints with escapes. The rule was measured byte for byte on the oracle, by printing `(intern (string C ?a ?b))` and `(intern (string ?a C ?b))` for every C from 1 to 127: bytes at or below the space, and `"#'(),;[]\` and the backquote, are escaped wherever they occur; the first byte is escaped when the whole name reads as a number, when the name starts with `?`, or when it starts with `.` and the next byte is not an ASCII letter. The last clause is why `.` and `..` are escaped and `.emacs` is not.

fe's `print` writes a TOP-LEVEL string bare -- `(print "abc")` is `abc` -- where Emacs' `print` writes `"abc"`. Nested strings are quoted on both sides, which is why every other string-valued case in this corpus agrees: the compat runner wraps each case in `(print EXPR)`, so only a case whose whole value is a string sees this. Fe's historical convention, unchanged by Phase 19 and deliberately not changed by it -- `print` is fe's `princ`-at-the-top spelling and the scripts' goldens are written in it. `cond-h2` is the case: it recorded `error-message-string`'s target rendering while the name was unsupported, and now that the name exists it measures this instead, byte for byte (`Wrong type argument: listp, 5` against Emacs' `"Wrong type argument: listp, 5"`). The rendering itself is measured by the five `error-message-string-*` cases, whose values are lists.
